questions.q: What two arguments does withColumn() take?
options: The new column's name, and a col()-based expression describing what goes in it
Only a single column name, with no expression
A file path and a schema
Two existing column names to merge together
questions.explain: This is exactly why Lesson 44 introduced col() early — it's needed to build the expression.

questions.q: What decides whether withColumn() adds a new column or replaces an existing one?
options: Whether the name passed already matches an existing column — same name replaces, new name adds
A separate replace=True flag must be passed
withColumn() can only ever add new columns, never replace
It depends on the column's data type
questions.explain: Nothing marks this differently syntactically — the name alone decides add vs. replace.

questions.q: Does trips.withColumn(...) modify the original trips DataFrame in place?
options: No — DataFrames are immutable, so it returns a new DataFrame, which is why the example reassigns trips = trips.withColumn(...)
Yes, it always mutates the original DataFrame directly
It depends on whether inferSchema was used when reading the data
Only if .cache() was called first
questions.explain: This connects straight back to Lesson 37's immutability property of Spark DataFrames.

questions.q: Can multiple withColumn() calls be chained together?
options: Yes — since each call returns a new DataFrame, chaining several in a row works normally
No, only one withColumn() call is allowed per DataFrame ever
Only if they're separated by a .collect() call in between
Chaining withColumn() calls always throws an error
questions.explain: This is the same chaining pattern Lesson 27's Pandas ETL script used.

questions.q: What kind of expression can go inside a withColumn() call?
options: Any expression built from col() references — arithmetic, comparisons, and conditional logic all work
Only a single literal number, nothing else
Only another column's exact values, unchanged
withColumn() cannot use expressions at all
questions.explain: This flexibility is exactly what makes withColumn() the core tool for building derived columns.
